summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla is an autonomous city of Spain and stands entirely under Spanish national law. Melilla has no autonomous LGTBI or gender-identity statute; an index of Spain's regional LGTBI legislation states expressly that Ceuta and Melilla have no autonomous laws of this kind and rely on the national framework and on central-government equality policies. Spanish criminal law, Spanish equality law and the Cuerpo Nacional de Policía govern in Melilla.

Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights throughout Spain, including Melilla. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the statute regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16. Legal gender change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Melilla as in the rest of Spain.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force nationwide since July 2005. The national framework also bans hate speech motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity, a prohibition dating from 1995, with crime-law penalty enhancements for such motives: the hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months. There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime; the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code.

Other operative provisions of the national statute reaching Melilla include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted-reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravating circumstance is documented at first-instance level in Spain. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case, fining a man EUR 300 for WhatsApp threats sent to a trans woman. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia in order to mock them; the single adult defendant received six months in prison and two minors were judged separately.

Sex-separated-space rules in Spain stand in contrast to the approach being adopted in the United Kingdom, where a stricter single-sex-space regime based on biological sex is applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

Administratively, Spain's self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change; that ranking is a dated baseline predating the 2023 statute.

A registry for unmarried same-sex couples was created in Melilla in 2008, following Ceuta in 1998 and the creation of equivalent registers in all 17 mainland autonomous communities. The benefits attached are regarded as mainly symbolic, and this registry is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute.
localsOnly:
Residents of Melilla obtain gender-marker rectification through the ordinary Civil Registry procedure set out in Article 43 of the national statute; no regional procedure or regional equality body exists, and the administrative route runs through state registries and ministries.

The national statute's resident-facing protections on anti-discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing, its ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, its expanded assisted-reproduction rules and its strengthened sexuality-education requirements apply in Melilla's schools, health services and workplaces on the same terms as elsewhere in Spain.

The consent regime for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and the conditions under which persons from age 12 may obtain recognition of their gender, are set nationally rather than by the Melilla assembly.

Law enforcement in Melilla is carried out by the Cuerpo Nacional de Policía under national command; criminal prosecution of offences with a gender-identity aggravating circumstance follows the national Criminal Code and the Ley Orgánica 6/2022 reforms.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents enforcement of the gender-identity aggravating circumstance, or any hate-crime or hate-speech conviction, within Melilla itself; the two dated enforcement examples on record come from courts in other Spanish cities and illustrate the national pattern only.

Facility rules are stated at the level of national law. Municipal practice in Melilla regarding access to gender-separated facilities in public buildings, schools or municipal services is not sourced.

Melilla's position as a border enclave means document and residency questions for third-country nationals and dual nationals living there are potentially decisive for a trans visitor or resident, but no source in this inventory addresses how Spanish gender-marker rules interact with foreign civil documents or with immigration status. This remains unresolved.

Availability of gender-affirming healthcare in Melilla, and any waiting times or referral requirements imposed by the Servicio Autónomo de Salud, are not sourced here. The comparison with the United Kingdom rests on a description of policy direction rather than a specific provision, and the 2016 attitudinal ranking predates the 2023 statute by seven years.
